title: Lakshmana's warning
hook: an apology, a flood of armies, and an embrace
carry: I may have slipped, who doesn't

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's warning met Tara's calm, and the anger cooled: this time somebody listens. Did you admit the true part first? Day five hundred ninety-three.

Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain. Sugriva is on his throne, dressed in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.
screen: `THE INNER PALACE.` → `SUGRIVA ON HIS THRONE.` → `HE GETS TO HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement. He repeats Rama's message. Sugriva doesn't argue. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped. Who doesn't? But I'm his friend and his servant, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness or overconfidence, forgive me. First idea: a good apology owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action. Sugriva does all three. Lakshmana softens at once. You've spoken well, he says. Come and see Rama. Second idea: the meeting. Sugriva rides out with Lakshmana to Rama, gets down, and bows with joined palms. Rama receives him with an embrace and asks him to sit beside him. Third: the armies arrive while they talk. Valmiki turns it into a parade. Monkeys and bears pour in past counting, from mountains and seashores, from forests and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth. The Sanskrit word for forgiveness, kshama, also means patience, and it's also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. Rama doesn't hold the lost weeks against him. The friendship is back where it was, and stronger, because now it has been tested and repaired. Sugriva now has an army ready to answer for him. And Rama turns to the real question: where do we look first?
screen: `NO ATONEMENT FOR INGRATITUDE.` · `SUGRIVA: FORGIVE ME.` · `AN EMBRACE, AND ARMIES.` · `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS, THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a small fault of yours that someone might still be holding. Breathe in, and own it privately and plainly: yes, I did that. Breathe out, and let yourself also be someone who can be forgiven. Then think of someone you could forgive, and let your hand open on your knee, palm up, for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana's warning. It ends in Sugriva's apology, a flood of armies, and Rama's embrace.
Your line: I may have slipped, who doesn't. Today, apologize for one small thing, and then do something about it. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the virtues in Hindu texts such as the Bhagavad Gita (16.3), and the reconciliation of Rama and Sugriva is told as an example of friendship repaired.

fork.setup: you're Sugriva. Lakshmana has just called you ungrateful. what do you say?
options: explain that you deserved a rest.
own the slip, ask forgiveness, and pledge your whole army.
fork.reveal: Sugriva apologizes plainly and pledges everything, and Lakshmana softens at once.

original.note: Sanskrit kṣamā: forgiveness, patience, forbearance; also a name for the earth, who bears everything.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sugriva just gets scolded.
what it means: he gives a real apology, and the friendship comes back stronger.
what a scholar hears: Lakshmana's words on ingratitude are in Kishkindha 34; Sugriva's apology in Kishkindha 36; the armies and Rama's embrace in Kishkindha 37–39.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 37–39 (the armies gather; Rama embraces Sugriva)
